clinicalPearls: Leukoplakia is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion: a white patch that cannot be wiped off and cannot be attributed to any other definable lesion
It is regarded as an oral potentially malignant disorder, meaning it carries an increased risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma
Tobacco use, including smokeless forms, areca nut, and alcohol are the principal risk factors
Homogeneous, uniformly white, flat lesions carry lower risk than non-homogeneous, nodular, or speckled (erythroleukoplakia) lesions
Speckled lesions with a red component and lesions on the floor of mouth or ventrolateral tongue have a higher malignant potential
Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is a distinct, multifocal, treatment-resistant form with high transformation risk
Biopsy is essential to assess for and grade epithelial dysplasia, which is the key predictor of malignant change
Management combines removal of risk factors, treatment or surveillance of the lesion, and long-term monitoring for recurrence or transformation
reference.pathophysiology: Leukoplakia reflects an alteration in the oral epithelium in which increased keratin production and epithelial thickening scatter light to produce a white appearance that does not rub off. Chronic exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco and areca nut drives genetic and epigenetic changes in basal keratinocytes, which may manifest histologically as hyperkeratosis with or without epithelial dysplasia. Dysplastic change represents disordered maturation and cellular atypia that can accumulate over time, and lesions with higher grades of dysplasia carry a greater likelihood of progressing to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
additionalInvestigations: Incisional or excisional biopsy for histological grading of dysplasia
Careful documentation of site, size, and clinical pattern
Removal of local irritants and reassessment to exclude frictional keratosis
Fungal investigation where hyperplastic candidiasis is suspected
Adjunctive imaging or referral when carcinoma is suspected
redFlags: Non-homogeneous, speckled, or verrucous lesions and any red component, indicating higher malignant potential
Ulceration, induration, or a developing mass suggesting transformation to carcinoma
High-risk sites such as the floor of mouth and ventrolateral tongue
Presence of moderate to severe epithelial dysplasia on biopsy
reference.prognosis: Many lesions remain stable or regress after risk factors are removed, but a proportion undergo malignant transformation, and the risk rises with non-homogeneous appearance, high-risk sites, and higher grades of dysplasia, making long-term surveillance important.
pitfalls: Labelling a white patch as benign without biopsy or follow-up
Assuming absence of symptoms means absence of risk
Sampling only a homogeneous area and missing dysplasia in a red or nodular component
Failing to address tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol use that perpetuate the lesion
management: Achieve cessation of tobacco (including smokeless forms), areca nut and alcohol, and remove local mechanical irritants
Perform incisional biopsy to grade dysplasia and exclude invasive carcinoma, using excisional biopsy for small lesions
Excise high-grade dysplastic, non-homogeneous or high-risk-site lesions (floor of mouth, ventrolateral tongue) by surgery or laser
Maintain long-term clinical surveillance with photographic documentation and re-biopsy of changing lesions given the malignant-transformation risk
Treat proliferative verrucous leukoplakia aggressively with close follow-up owing to its high transformation rate
Refer to oral medicine or head and neck services when carcinoma is suspected
